chapter_theme: Stories of the Linga Purana (இலிங்க புராணம்): the mountain's daughter, Vishnu and Brahma, Ravana, Chandesa and the gods each worshipped or submitted and received the Lord's grace; the Lord who destroyed the three cities is not hard to reach, and is not false to those who love him.
structure_note: A string of puranic episodes (347, 349 to 352) around one assurance (348): the Lord is not out of reach for those with devotion.

347.reading: Resolving to reach his feet and looking to our First, she became the daughter of the crowned mountain-king, did firm tapas, and, as the gods knew, worshipped him fully on earth and gave him devotion.
347.nuance: The goddess is unnamed; the mountain's daughter is Parvati. Even the Lord's consort reaches him by tapas and worship, the means open to devotees.

348.reading: Do not grow weary thinking the Lord who destroyed the wandering three cities is hard to reach; the Lord is not false to those who love him, and he stands with tenderness and knows their worth.
348.nuance: புரிவுடையார், those with புரிவு, may be those with love, with longing, or with understanding. பரிசறிவான் may be 'knows their worth' or 'knows what to give them'.

349.reading: When Brahma and Vishnu circled the sea and did reverence through an age, the bright-flamed First gave the discus to Achyuta in that way, and gave a sword to Brahma as well.
349.nuance: ஆழி may be the sea or the wheel, and வலம் circling or power; the first two lines are hard to fix. The gift of the discus to Vishnu is a known legend; the sword to Brahma is less familiar.

350.reading: He who bore twenty arms and lifted the great mountain high had a matchless strength; when the Lord crushed him there and he cried 'Hara!', the Stainless One gave him unending grace.
350.nuance: Ravana is not named. The verse moves from pride in strength to a single cry and to grace that does not leave: the crushing is the first step of grace.

351.reading: Chandi, who knew what was coming, heaped fine sand and bathed it with the five products of the cow; when his father came in hostility and wrecked it, he grew angry, cut him with the axe, and received a garland.
351.nuance: The legend of Chandesa, the cowherd boy who worshipped a sand linga and struck his father's leg when he kicked it over, and was made chief of the Lord's servants and given his garland. அறுவகை (six kinds) and உறுவது அறி are unclear. The verse reports the act and the reward without comment.

352.reading: The gods all ran together, faces withered, went in distress, sought him and bowed saying 'Lord, we bow'; the One of matchless fame said 'Rise'.
352.nuance: The occasion is not named; it is often taken as the poison rising from the churned ocean. நம என்று may be the 'namah' of worship.

links.note: 343 calls fools those who say he burned three cities, meaning the cities are the impurities; 348 still names him the destroyer of the three cities, so the epithet stands and only its literal sense is questioned.

197 makes not killing the finest flower of worship; 351 tells, with approval shown by the reward, of a devotee who cut down his own father to protect his worship. The conflict depends on reading 351 as commending the act rather than only reporting a legend.

348 tells the reader not to tire thinking the Lord is hard to reach (அரியனென்று எண்ணி அயர்வுற வேண்டா): he is not false to those who love him (புரிவுடையாளர்க்குப் பொய்யலன்). 309 says the First comes near only to those who know him with longing (நச்சு உணர்ந்தார்க்கே நணுகலுமாமே). Both make love the one condition of his nearness; 348 says it as reassurance, 309 as restriction.

source_issues: 351 line 2 (அறுவகை ஆன்ஐந்தும்) is unclear; அறுவகை may be corrupt.
